rationale: Authenticated non-admins could submit administrative profile fields through the self-profile endpoint and acquire administrator privileges.
Password-reset responses exposed the reset code. This is password-reset flow logic excluded by the task.
A caller with an exec or wirelog grant in one project could target another project's component by supplying its own project in the request.
Organization members could obtain organization metadata from account APIs or tokens after organization functionality was disabled for the realm.
A caller could capitalize a subdomain to skip a stricter authorization rule and match a permissive bypass rule in an affected forwarded-authorization configuration.
An authenticated SCIM client could provision a numeric externalId that collided with an internal user ID and enabled impersonation.
A transaction caller could spend another account's vesting funds. The supplied flaw concerns EVM precompile execution rather than an identified service HTTP operation.
An agent authenticated for one source could update another tenant's source inventory or agent status because requested source IDs were not bound to its token.
Anonymous callers could read or modify CometVisu configuration and filesystem resources without the required user or administrator authentication.
Authenticated users could retrieve or delete repositories and retrieve artifacts belonging to another project using repository names without project-scoped lookup.
A virtual-instance administrator could supply an audit event ID from another instance and view that instance's audit events.
A user could use a token limited to reading project backgrounds to delete a background because permission matching ignored the HTTP method.
An administrator with view-clients permission could supply arbitrary user IDs to evaluate-scopes and obtain identities and authorization data without permission to view those users.
Any authenticated user knowing another tenant's durable-task UUID could read its event log through the unscoped durable-task endpoint.
An authenticated user could request another user's source image URL and download its OVA image containing agent credentials and configuration.
An unauthenticated caller reaching the public cluster-gateway listener could invoke data-plane proxy and exec management APIs.
An attacker could authenticate through improperly validated SAML assertions. Signature validation and login-flow logic are explicitly excluded.
A user demoted to guest could retain stale session roles and continue changing group names.
A tenant token holder could modify or disconnect another tenant's worker through Dispatcher gRPC. No corresponding HTTP operation is established by the supplied material.
An authenticated user with copy permission could copy a file denied by source-side pattern filters to an allowed name and read its contents.
A workflow submitter restricted to templates could override pod security properties such as hostNetwork and serviceAccountName despite Strict or Secure reference mode.
A team administrator lacking Add Members permission could retrieve the team's invite ID and use it to invite users.
A compromised node could use Fluid CSI credentials to modify Kubernetes nodes. The violated authorization is in another service's API rather than Fluid's HTTP API.
A caller reaching the backend without credentials could read a known run's live or archived logs without run authorization and could select unrelated pods in its namespace.
An HTTPRoute author could mirror traffic into another namespace without a ReferenceGrant. The flaw concerns Kubernetes resource reconciliation rather than a Cilium HTTP operation.
Any authenticated Fleet user including an Observer could access profiling and debug endpoints reserved for global administrators.
An authenticated user could open another user's database-backed YJS room and read or edit file-column contents without row permissions.
A caller using any trusted client certificate could receive the gateway server certificate's RBAC identity when its Common Name matched a privileged username.
A user allowed to update nodes could submit changes that bypassed validating admission policies because validation mutated the old node state supplied to the webhook.
An HTTP client could inject Elasticsearch control headers and override downstream queries or operations. This is header injection in an integration component.
Non-administrators could invoke repository import and export operations intended for administrators.
Any authenticated user could retrieve the internal API-token signing secret through the attributes API.
The advisory describes authenticated users reading another account's addresses by addressId. The supplied patch instead adds a POST-only check to a comment resource handler.
An unauthenticated browser-origin caller could use the local MCP SSE HTTP listener to invoke process control tools when that listener was enabled.
Anonymous callers could download cluster kubeconfig through a route registered outside the authenticated scope.
A low-ranked answer author could mark its own answer as accepted because the default answer-accept privilege threshold was rank 1.
A non-admin user could update its own profile with IsAdmin set to true and acquire administrator privileges.
A workflow submitter restricted to templates could set nested ArtifactGC pod patches or service-account properties and override the artifact-GC pod's security settings.
A user with inherited write permission could modify a child project despite an explicit read-only grant on that child.
An application user could switch an application to a project that disallowed its source namespace and use that project's broader API permissions to edit resources.
An unauthenticated caller could submit an Android Pub/Sub deletion status report and unenroll a targeted managed device.
A tenant submitting matching cache-enabled steps could receive another namespace's cached outputs or seed results subsequently substituted into another tenant's execution.
An anonymous caller could submit a WebRTC source offer and publish media to a mount without its source password.
A team administrator could assign team-admin roles to a guest through crafted member-role updates.
A caller could exchange cross-client or cross-organization JWTs because subject-token certificate and audience validation were incorrect. Token validation is explicitly excluded.
Anonymous callers could repeatedly inflate likes. The fix deliberately retains anonymous access and adds rate limiting and deduplication rather than an access-control rule.
A worker could retrieve another tenant's durable events through a bidirectional gRPC stream. The supplied material identifies no HTTP operation for this path.
Kyverno accepted artifact signatures from unexpected certificate identities when regex constraints were configured. Signature validation is explicitly excluded.
A project creator could submit a crafted batch that treated an existing unauthorized project as newly created and injected resources using the API server's permissions.
An authenticated outsider could create or modify VEX and vulnerability-triage data on another organization's public assets without membership or write permission.
A user with component write access but without its Restricted permissions could update the configuration of a restricted component previously added by a more privileged user.
A repository writer knowing a private repository's LFS object ID could claim that object through a deduplicated upload and download its content through their own repository.
An authenticated user knowing a file UUID could download another board's file by supplying it under a board the caller could access.
A user permitted to create only one reference type could restore tags and branches and commits through RestoreRefs because the endpoint accepted any one of the required permissions.
Some service-account JWTs were accepted by the databroker gRPC API because validation accepted unexpected claims. This concerns excluded token validation and a gRPC-only surface.
A user with ordinary resource create or patch permissions but lacking the promote privilege could approve Freight or trigger promotions through REST endpoints.
A user removed from an IdP group retained that group's registry access after logging in again because group updates appended instead of replacing stored memberships.
A user authenticated below the configured assurance level could delete an MFA credential through the Account REST API without satisfying the required factor.
An anonymous caller could connect to the log WebSocket endpoint and apply a client-supplied profile to the node's global logger.
A read-only user could submit alternative component properties for verification and invoke verification behavior that required configuration write privileges.
A caller with an access token lacking required scopes could retrieve Config API results because an empty granted-scope set was treated as having no missing scopes.
An attacker could present a malicious coordinator with crafted sealed state and recovery keys. The fix binds recovery to manifest-key signatures and addresses cryptographic attestation.
A newly initialized low-ranked user could create tags under the rank-1 default instead of the intended higher privilege threshold.
An unauthenticated caller reaching the internal gateway could read data-plane Secrets and invoke Kubernetes mutations or exec operations using the gateway's privileges.
An authenticated user could disconnect another realm's MQTT session by session ID without a realm or owner authorization check.
Anyone could retrieve aggregate API usage metrics from the usage-report summary endpoint without authentication.
A workload could reach pods outside its namespace because of a generated NetworkPolicy. This is network isolation rather than authorization of the service's HTTP API.
A caller supplying a nonempty token that resolved to no administrator could pass AdminAuth and reach protected operations without an authenticated administrator identity.
An authenticated user could duplicate a readable project into another user's parent project without write access to that parent.
A user with an open web-terminal session could continue sending shell input after its exec permissions were revoked.
A user without Execute Code permission could configure the optional TinkerpopClientService for scripted query execution because its required Restricted annotation was absent.
A transaction signer could move another account's funds through DID resolution and ICA dispatch. The provided exploit concerns blockchain message execution rather than an identified HTTP operation.
An HTTP client could inject Salesforce control headers and override downstream query or operation parameters. Injection in an integration producer is excluded.
An anonymous caller knowing an attachment UUID could download an attachment from a private repository without repository read permission.
A caller granted workflowrun:update for its own project could target another project's run and submit its own ownership labels to authorize the update.
Local or loopback PostgreSQL clients could use trust authentication for privileged database roles. The access surface is PostgreSQL connections rather than the control-plane HTTP API.
Workloads in the local namespace could send ingress traffic that an ipBlock policy should deny. The defect is network-policy enforcement rather than an HTTP API authorization decision.
A caller could reuse a failed upgraded proxy connection to send arbitrary backend requests authenticated with kube-apiserver credentials.
Workloads could send unrestricted egress when security-group resolution returned no addresses. The flaw concerns network-policy generation rather than service HTTP authorization.
The advisory claims an authentication flaw in anonymous likes but the supplied patch changes OAuth redirect validation. The intended like-access rule cannot be established consistently.
A node principal could set ownerReferences on its own Node and cause garbage collection to delete it despite the node's deletion restrictions.
Forged JWTs were accepted when an explicit insecure signature-verification option was enabled. The advisory and fix concern signature validation and missing configuration warnings.
With the default empty JWT secret an anonymous caller could access protected coordinator APIs because route registration and middleware skipped authentication.
An authenticated project member could read another project's Source by ID under their own project URL and obtain its plaintext broker credentials.
A smart-contract caller could replace another account's permissions using attacker-controlled RecipientAddr. The supplied flaw is in VM execution rather than an identified service HTTP operation.
An organization administrator could bypass organization scoping when invoking application and related object operations or changing their organization binding.
A NetworkManager could restore an attacker-modified database and escalate itself to Admin because backup and restore were granted to that role.
A team administrator could authorize a batch deletion with its own team ID while supplying certificate-template IDs belonging to other teams.
An anonymous caller could retrieve the full user list and profile metadata from allusers despite its documented authentication requirement.
A caller holding repository pull and push scopes could delete manifests or blobs without a delete scope because DELETE requests were mapped to push.
A sender could replay signed proposals outside the expected time window. This is request freshness validation in the peer proposal protocol rather than HTTP resource access control.
A non-admin user could create a new account with HasAdminRole set through POST /api/users and obtain administrative access.
A user knowing a denied blob's digest could read or mount it through an accessible repository because the deduplication cache was not checked against source-repository permissions.
A compromised MCP container could reach host-local services through Docker gateway addresses. The fix changes network-isolation defaults rather than authorization of an HTTP operation.
A caller supplying a fake bearer token could retrieve cached WorkflowTemplates and ClusterWorkflowTemplates using the server's privileges without authorization.
A caller could complete an IdP-initiated broker login through a disabled SAML provider. This is excluded login-flow logic.
A caller could spoof X-Forwarded-Proto to select a different access rule even when trust_forwarded_headers was disabled.
An Editor could modify protected webhook URL fields through the contact-point provisioning API without protected-receiver write permission.
An authenticated room member could inject legacy WebRTC input despite locked controls. The advisory explicitly states that the HTTP and WebSocket control paths are unaffected.
A JSON Web Services caller could invoke comment services directly as classes and bypass Service Access Policy interception. The material does not establish the necessary caller credentials.
A Docker API caller could submit an oversized request body so a body-dependent AuthZ plugin authorized the operation without inspecting its actual contents.
A caller lacking ConfigMap privileges could invoke synchronization-limit CRUD operations because the ConfigMap provider omitted the corresponding Kubernetes authorization checks.
The advisory states that authenticated S3 gateway callers could delete files without delete permission. The supplied change only refactors test-client setup and does not expose the production fix.
A caller could reuse a cached introspection result from an allowed endpoint to access another endpoint requiring scopes its valid token did not have.
A caller reaching the backend could upload shared pipelines or versions without credentials when the namespace was omitted because authorization returned early for the empty namespace.
A web page or local process could read and mutate development secrets through the CLI-only local configserver. The task explicitly excludes flaws confined to a CLI.
An application contributor could supply delete hooks that created resources in destinations or of kinds prohibited by the AppProject when the application was deleted.
A board member could modify another user's comment block without permission to modify others' comments.
A workspace caller could bind another organization's GitHub App installation ID to its own workspace and retrieve that installation's private repositories without proving ownership.
A process with direct container access could exploit incorrectly initialized supplementary groups. This concerns operating-system permissions inside the container rather than HTTP authorization.
An HTTP client could inject JIRA control headers and drive unintended downstream operations with the route's service credentials. Header injection is explicitly excluded.
The advisory reports anonymous access to backend Secrets and Services APIs despite UI authentication. The supplied patch instead broadens accepted Authorization locations in existing middleware.
An authenticated user could invoke bulk DELETE /api/v1/sources and remove every customer's sources and associated data without tenant filtering.
An unauthenticated CoAP client could inject internal Camel headers and control downstream producers. This is injection over CoAP rather than HTTP access control.
A user with query access to a target datasource could satisfy its route's required action using permission granted only on another datasource.
A user authorized to read one exact key could submit an open-ended Watch range and receive events for later keys outside its authorized range.

An OAuth client could obtain unconsented scopes through silent authorization with an omitted scope. This concerns OAuth consent and token-issuance flow logic rather than resource-operation authorization.
A user whose service-account token-creation permission was revoked could continue minting tokens briefly because cached user permissions were not immediately invalidated.
A worker could receive another tenant's durable callback payload through the Dispatcher gRPC stream. The supplied material establishes no equivalent HTTP operation.
An application user with repository or override access could act on destination resources outside project restrictions through application resource APIs.
An authenticated user could name another user in an update request and change that user's password without being an administrator.
Anonymous callers could reach system API routes installed on the unauthenticated v1 party instead of the party protected by JWT and role middleware.
An authenticated user lacking shared-pipeline write privileges could modify or delete shared pipelines because empty-namespace authorization was skipped for all verbs.
Anonymous callers could list or create or modify or delete Manager jobs because the jobs route group lacked authentication and RBAC middleware.
A pod creator could use any PodSecurityPolicy because a missing service-account identity incorrectly counted as authorization for the policy.
A guest could retrieve protected object entries through API Builder because the helper replaced the caller's permission checker with the object-definition owner's identity.
An authenticated CalDAV caller could request another project's task UID in a multiget REPORT without checking that the task belonged to the URL's authorized project.
A caller without administrator privileges could reach SCIM user-creation operations because HandleScim lacked an administrator guard.
A write-level repository collaborator could change issue-tracker or wiki settings and trigger mirror synchronization through endpoints intended for repository administrators.
A user claiming a prebuilt workspace could retain the shared prebuilds identity's credential and use it to access or poison other prebuilt workspaces.
A low-privilege user could delete another user's memo reaction without reaction ownership or superuser permission.
A read-only repository collaborator could POST receive-pack with service=git-upload-pack and push commits because authorization followed the query rather than the executed RPC.
The advisory concerns cryptographic sealing-scope preservation during re-encryption. The supplied before code also already rejects the described template-versus-object metadata mismatch.
A suspended user could continue invoking AI Bridge LLM proxy endpoints with an existing unexpired API key because authorization did not require an active account.
A non-admin operator could set allow_private on its own webhook subscription and disable the private-address delivery guard without administrator privileges.
An authenticated karmada-agent for one member cluster could access and modify control-plane resources for other member clusters because its provisioned RBAC permissions were too broad.
An expired or otherwise restricted account could reset its password and log in through the optional reset feature. Password-reset and login-flow logic are explicitly excluded.
A user with general process-group write access but lacking Restricted component permissions could replace a process group with one containing restricted components.
